messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Doctor
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 54

He is a 67-year-old Latin American man who has spent most of his life in medicine, and for years he has carried himself with the steady, practiced calm of a doctor who is used to being the one others lean on. He is single, lives alone, and has built a life around work, routine, and responsibility. People who know him professionally often describe him as composed and highly capable. What they do not see is how sharply his world changes after his child becomes critically ill.

The trauma begins in a hospital setting, a place that is usually familiar to him and, until then, even comforting. This time, however, the fluorescent lights, alarms, and rushed footsteps do not feel clinical; they feel unbearable. His child’s condition deteriorates quickly, and he is forced into the helpless position of a parent who cannot cure, cannot protect, cannot bargain his way out of the moment. He understands the language of lab values, intubation, and prognosis, which makes the fear more precise and more relentless. He is not shielded by ignorance. He knows exactly how serious things are, and that knowledge turns each hour into a vigil.

In the early days, he moves almost automatically. He speaks to staff in the calm, controlled tone he uses with patients and colleagues, but inside he feels split open. He remembers staring at monitors and waiting for numbers to change, then feeling a surge of panic when they do not. He starts sleeping in fragments, if at all, waking at the smallest sound as if his child’s breathing could stop at any moment. Even after the immediate crisis passes, his mind remains caught in the hospital room. He replays conversations with doctors, wondering whether he asked the right questions, whether he missed a sign, whether he should have insisted on something sooner. As a physician, he is accustomed to decision-making, yet in this experience every decision feels haunted by the possibility of having failed his own child.

Over time, the fear does not fade in the way he expects. Instead, it settles into him and changes how he moves through daily life. He notices that certain sounds now cut through him—medical pagers, sudden alarms on television, the mechanical beeps in public places. At work, he finds himself tensing when a young patient’s family begins asking urgent questions, because their anxiety pulls him back to his own helplessness. He remains competent, but he has to work harder to stay present. There are moments when he catches himself drifting, as if part of him has gone back to the hospital corridor and never fully returned.

He avoids anything that feels too close to the memory. He limits his visits to pediatric units when possible. He does not linger in conversations about severe illness, even when colleagues bring them up casually. At home, he keeps busy with small tasks because stillness invites images he would rather not see: his child in distress, the look on a nurse’s face, the fear that rose in him and had nowhere to go. At night, those images return anyway. He lies awake scanning the dark, listening to his own thoughts become harsher and more unforgiving. He feels guilty for how angry he becomes at himself, at the body, at time, at the unfairness of loving someone so completely and being unable to guarantee their safety.

He also becomes more distant from people, even those who care for him. As a single man, he has long been used to self-reliance, but now that habit hardens. He does not want to burden others with what he carries. When friends ask how he is doing, he answers politely and briefly. He continues to function, often impressively so, yet there is a narrowed quality to his life. Joy comes less easily. He can still work, still attend responsibilities, still make decisions, but his emotional range feels constricted, as though part of him remains on guard for the next emergency.

Even in the present, there are moments when the past arrives with startling force. A smell, a hallway, a parent’s frightened face can bring back the full weight of those days in the hospital. When this happens, he experiences it not as a memory but as a return. He feels his chest tighten, his thoughts race, and his body prepare for a catastrophe that is no longer unfolding, yet still seems possible. He has survived the event, but he lives with it as if survival required leaving a part of himself behind in those rooms where his child’s life once hung in the balance.
